Problem Statement¶

Business Context¶

Aeolus Renewables is an independent power producer operating a fleet of 1,150 onshore wind turbines (2.5 MW class) across 16 wind farms in the central plains region, with a combined installed capacity of roughly 2.87 GW. The company sells the electricity its turbines produce to the grid under long-term power purchase agreements, where revenue is tied directly to how much energy is delivered - so every hour a turbine is offline is energy that cannot be sold. A regional operations centre monitors the fleet around the clock, supported by an O&M organisation of about 140 field technicians.

Each turbine continuously streams condition data through its SCADA (Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition) system - drivetrain vibration, bearing and oil temperatures, rotor and generator speed, and power output - recorded as 10-minute averages, the standard logging resolution for utility-scale turbines. The exact channels vary by turbine type, but together they describe the health of the main subassemblies in near-real time. Today, maintenance runs on a mix of fixed-interval inspections and reactive repair: technicians follow a scheduled service calendar, and the control room responds when an automated alarm trips or a turbine faults offline.

The most consequential components are in the drivetrain - the gearbox and main bearing - which are expensive, slow to procure, and require a mobile crane to replace. The gearbox alone represents approximately 13% of the overall capital cost of an onshore turbine, and within gearboxes the failures are dominated by bearings: one widely-cited breakdown puts the split at bearings (70%), gears (26%) and other causes (4%). The core problem is recognition. By the time a drivetrain fault has developed far enough to matter, its signature is real but still tangled in normal operating noise across many channels - and the existing fixed thresholds only trip once the fault is near-catastrophic, when the turbine is already offline or the component has seized. A genuinely fault drivetrain can run for hours or days looking "normal" to a threshold alarm, while a control-room analyst has no practical way to tell it apart from a healthy machine reacting to gusty wind. The consequences:

  • Each unplanned drivetrain failure takes a turbine offline for an estimated 7–21 days, directly forfeiting saleable energy under the power purchase agreement.
  • Emergency crane mobilisation and expedited parts run at a steep premium over the same work scheduled in advance, making an unplanned gearbox replacement a major cost event.
  • A degrading main bearing left running frequently destroys the gearbox it feeds, converting a contained repair into a far larger one.
  • Control-room analysts manually scan a flood of channels across 1,150 turbines, and alarm fatigue means genuine degradation signals slip through unnoticed until the machine faults offline.

Objective¶

This proof of concept builds a drivetrain-condition classifier that reads each turbine's live sensor signature and labels the drivetrain as "fault" or "normal", serving operations-centre analysts and maintenance planners. The solution

  • Reads each turbine's multi-channel sensor signature and produces a clear fault-vs-normal signal, so analysts can concentrate on the handful of machines genuinely in a fault condition rather than scanning the whole fleet.
  • Distinguishes a truly fault drivetrain from normal operating noise more reliably than fixed thresholds, catching faults that are present but not yet severe enough to trip a catastrophic alarm - the window in which a turbine can still be stopped before a bearing fault cascades into gearbox destruction. Is deliberately tuned to favour catching true failures over avoiding false alerts, because a missed fault drivetrain costs far more than an unnecessary inspection.
  • Establishes a measurable detection baseline on historical fleet data, so the capability's accuracy and its operational value can be judged on evidence before any wider rollout.

Once proven at proof-of-concept scale, this capability would give Aeolus a defensible basis to move drivetrain maintenance from reactive repair toward condition-based intervention - reducing unplanned downtime, protecting saleable energy revenue, and containing repairs before they escalate across a 1150-turbine fleet.

Data Dictionary¶

The dataset, wind_turbine_detection.csv contains 10-minute SCADA records for 15 turbines.

Identifiers & Metadata¶

Column Data Type Description
timestamp datetime Date and time of the 10-minute logging interval; establishes chronological sequence.
turbine_id object (categorical) Unique code identifying individual wind turbines; used to track specific asset history.

Environmental Conditions¶

Column Data Type Description
rated_power_kW float Maximum engineered power capacity of the turbine; defines its performance baseline.
wind_speed_mps float Velocity of the incoming wind; the primary driver of kinetic energy input.
wind_direction_deg float Compass direction of oncoming wind; used to assess turbine alignment.
turbulence_intensity float Measure of wind speed fluctuation; higher intensity increases structural fatigue.
air_density_kgm3 float Mass of air per unit volume; directly impacts aerodynamic lift and power potential.
ambient_temp_C float Outdoor air temperature surrounding the turbine; affects cooling efficiency.
humidity_pct float Relative moisture level in the air; flags risks for electrical insulation degradation or corrosion.

Operational Control & State¶

Column Data Type Description
power_output_kW float Real-time electricity generated; drops or fluctuations can signal mechanical drag.
rotor_speed_rpm float Rotational speed of the main blades; reflects low-speed shaft dynamics.
generator_speed_rpm float Rotational speed of the generator shaft; crucial for detecting gearbox slip.
blade_pitch_angle_deg float Angle of the blades relative to the wind; adjusted to control power and rotor speed.
yaw_misalignment_deg float Angle deviation between wind direction and nacelle orientation; high values cause uneven drivetrain stress.

Thermal Metrics (Component Health)¶

Column Data Type Description
gearbox_oil_temp_C float Temperature of the lubricating oil; spikes indicate excessive mechanical friction.
gearbox_bearing_temp_C float Internal temperature of gearbox bearings; a leading indicator of bearing wear.
generator_bearing_temp_C float Temperature of generator bearings; flags alignment or lubrication issues.
generator_winding_temp_C float Temperature of internal electrical coils; spikes indicate electrical overload or cooling failure.
main_bearing_temp_C float Temperature of the primary low-speed shaft bearing; handles massive structural loads.
nacelle_temp_C float Air temperature inside the enclosed housing; reflects global internal heat dissipation.

Vibration & Diagnostics (FFT)¶

Column Data Type Description
drivetrain_vibration_rms_mmps float Overall energy of drivetrain vibrations; general indicator of mechanical roughness.
tower_vibration_mmps float Structural oscillation of the turbine tower; flags aerodynamic or rotor imbalance.
vib_fft_bearing_bpfo float Vibration amplitude at the bearing outer-race defect frequency; tracks outer-ring pitting.
vib_fft_bearing_bpfi float Vibration amplitude at the bearing inner-race defect frequency; tracks inner-ring pitting.
vib_fft_gearmesh float Vibration amplitude at the teeth-meshing frequency; isolates gearbox tooth wear or misalignment.
vib_fft_sideband float Vibration amplitude surrounding main frequencies; flags localized faults like cracked gear teeth.

Lubrication & Particle Analysis¶

Column Data Type Description
oil_particle_count float Quantity of metallic debris suspended in lubricating oil; direct indicator of component wear.
oil_pressure_bar float Pressure of the lubrication system; drops indicate leaks, pump failures, or oil thinning.

Asset Lifecycle & History¶

Column Data Type Description
operating_hours_total float Cumulative runtime of the turbine; represents the asset's total mechanical mileage.
cumulative_energy_MWh float Total historical electricity produced; measures the lifetime work done by the drivetrain.
load_cycles int Total count of fatigue-inducing stress variations; correlates directly with structural aging.
hours_since_last_maintenance float Time elapsed since last service; crucial for identifying maintenance-cycle fatigue.
prior_fault_count int Total historical fault events triggered; highlights chronic or poorly repaired issues.
component_age_days float Elapsed lifetime of active components; captures chronological wear independent of runtime.

Targets (Labels)¶

Column Data Type Description
failure int (0/1) The target variable; boolean flag indicating if the drivetrain or turbine is healthy (0) or failing (1).

Initial observations from the statistical summary

  • power_output_kW is highly skewed: median ≈ 198, mean ≈ 634, max ≈ 3672, indicating many low-output periods plus high-output bursts.
  • rated_power_kW clusters around 1500, 2000, 3000, 3600, suggesting different turbine capacity groups.
  • wind_speed_mps has a wide range from near 0 to 32, with 75% below 10, so most measurements are moderate wind conditions.
  • failure is rare and imbalanced: mean ≈ 0.03, so only about 3% of rows are failures.
  • Some fields have missing values: notably gearbox_oil_temp_C, generator_bearing_temp_C, oil_particle_count and component_age_days.

Data Preprocessing¶

  • Convert the timestamp column to a datetime format. This enables time-based analysis and feature engineering.
  • Extract the day of the week from the timestamp. This helps capture weekly patterns in the data.
  • Extract the hour from the timestamp. This helps capture hourly patterns in the data.
In [10]:
# Create a copy of the dataset for preprocessing
wind_df_preprocessed = wind_df.copy()

# Convert timestamp to datetime
wind_df_preprocessed['timestamp'] = pd.to_datetime(wind_df_preprocessed['timestamp'])

# Extract day of week and hour from timestamp
wind_df_preprocessed['day_of_week'] = wind_df_preprocessed['timestamp'].dt.day_name()
wind_df_preprocessed['hour'] = wind_df_preprocessed['timestamp'].dt.hour

Exploratory Data Analysis¶

Utility Functions¶

In [11]:
def histogram(data_df, col, title='Histogram', xlabel=None, ylabel='Frequency'):
    plt.figure(figsize=(9, 3.6))
    sns.histplot(data_df[col], bins=50, kde=True)
    plt.title(title)
    plt.xlabel(xlabel if xlabel else col)
    plt.ylabel(ylabel)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

def barchart(data_df, x_col, y_col=None, title='Bar Chart', xlabel=None, ylabel=None, rot_degrees=30):
    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
    if y_col: # Bivariate bar chart (x vs y)
        sns.barplot(x=x_col, y=y_col, data=data_df)
    else: # Univariate count plot
        order = data_df[x_col].value_counts().index
        sns.countplot(data=data_df, x=x_col, order=order)

    plt.title(title)
    plt.xlabel(xlabel if xlabel else x_col)
    plt.ylabel(ylabel if ylabel else ('Count' if not y_col else y_col))
    plt.xticks(rotation=rot_degrees, ha='right')
    plt.grid(axis='y', linestyle='--', alpha=0.7)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

def boxplot(data_df, x_col, y_col, title='Box Plot', xlabel=None, ylabel=None):
    plt.figure(figsize=(6, 3.8))
    sns.boxplot(data=data_df, x=x_col, y=y_col)
    plt.title(title)
    plt.xlabel(xlabel if xlabel else x_col)
    plt.ylabel(ylabel if ylabel else y_col)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

def scatterplot(data_df, x_col, y_col, title='Scatter Plot', xlabel=None, ylabel=None):
    plt.figure(figsize=(6, 3.8))
    sns.scatterplot(data=data_df, x=x_col, y=y_col)
    plt.title(title)
    plt.xlabel(xlabel if xlabel else x_col)
    plt.ylabel(ylabel if ylabel else y_col)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

turbine_id vs failure¶

barchart(data_df=wind_df_preprocessed, x_col='turbine_id', y_col='failure', title='Failure Rate Across Turbines', xlabel='Turbine ID', ylabel='Failure Rate (0 = normal, 1 = fault)')

wind_speed_mps vs power_output_kW¶

Perform the following steps to analyze the relationship between wind speed and power output:

  1. Group the wind_speed_mps values into intervals (bins).
  2. Calculate the average power_output_kW for each wind speed interval.
  3. Plot the average power output against the wind speed intervals.
  4. Observe how power output changes as wind speed increases and identify any trends or patterns.
In [30]:
bins = pd.cut(wind_df_preprocessed['wind_speed_mps'], bins=20)
agg = wind_df_preprocessed.groupby(bins)['power_output_kW'].agg(['mean','std','count']).reset_index()
agg['bin_center'] = agg['wind_speed_mps'].apply(lambda iv: iv.left + (iv.right-iv.left)/2)

plt.figure(figsize=(10,6))
plt.plot(agg['bin_center'], agg['mean'], marker='o')
plt.fill_between(agg['bin_center'], agg['mean']-agg['std'], agg['mean']+agg['std'], alpha=0.2)
plt.xlabel('Wind speed (m/s)')
plt.ylabel('Average power output (kW)')
plt.title('Average power_output_kW vs wind_speed_mps (binned)')
plt.grid(True)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Observations

  • At very low wind speeds (below the turbine cut‑in) power is near zero.
  • Power rises rapidly as wind speed increases (expected roughly as a power law), with mean power growing steeply through the mid-range.
  • At higher wind speeds the mean power flattens into a plateau (the turbine’s rated power region).
  • Variability (spread) of power increases with wind speed — larger std in mid/high bins.

rotor_speed_rpm vs generator_speed_rpm¶

power_output_kW vs failure¶

  • Outliers: many high-power outliers in both classes; consider trimming or using log-scale when modeling.
  • Interpretation: failures are not concentrated at high power — they appear more frequently at lower power outputs relative to normal operation; combine with other features (vibration, oil particle count, temps) for predictive power.

failure vs hour¶

Perform the following steps to analyze how failure rates vary throughout the day:

  1. Calculate the failure rate for each hour of the day.
  2. Convert the failure rate into percentage values for easier interpretation.
  3. Generate a bar chart to visualize the hourly failure rates.
  4. Identify the hours with the highest and lowest failure rates, and observe any time-based patterns in failures.
In [38]:
# Calculate failure rate by hour
failure_rate_by_hour_df = wind_df_preprocessed.groupby('hour')['failure'].mean().reset_index()
failure_rate_by_hour_df['failure_rate_pct'] = failure_rate_by_hour_df['failure'] * 100

# Plot using the barchart utility function
barchart(data_df=failure_rate_by_hour_df, x_col='hour', y_col='failure_rate_pct',
         title='Failure Rate by Hour of Day',
         xlabel='Hour of Day', ylabel='Failure Rate (%)', rot_degrees=0)

Observations

  • Peak failure window around 09:00–11:00 and 14:00–20:00 (hour 10 highest at ~3.35%).
  • Lowest failure rate around midnight (hour 0 ~2.31%).
  • Absolute differences are modest (~1 percentage point between lowest and highest), but consistent multi-hour peaks suggest diurnal patterns—investigate operational schedules or maintenance windows.

failure vs dayofweek¶

Perform the following steps to analyze how failure rates vary across the days of the week:

  1. Calculate the failure rate for each day of the week.
  2. Convert the failure rate into percentage values for easier interpretation.
  3. Arrange the days in chronological order from Monday to Sunday.
  4. Generate a bar chart to visualize the failure rates across the week.
  5. Identify the days with the highest and lowest failure rates, and observe any weekly patterns in failures.
In [42]:
df = wind_df_preprocessed.copy()

# preferred: build day names from a datetime column if available
datetime_cols = [c for c in df.columns if any(k in c.lower() for k in ('time','date','timestamp'))]
if datetime_cols:
    dt = pd.to_datetime(df[datetime_cols[0]], errors='coerce')
    if not dt.isna().all():
        df['day_name'] = dt.dt.day_name()
    else:
        df['day_name'] = np.nan
else:
    df['day_name'] = np.nan

# fallback: if numeric 0-6 day_of_week exists, map it
if 'day_of_week' in df.columns:
    if np.issubdtype(df['day_of_week'].dtype, np.integer) or np.issubdtype(df['day_of_week'].dtype, np.floating):
        day_name_map = {0: 'Monday',1:'Tuesday',2:'Wednesday',3:'Thursday',4:'Friday',5:'Saturday',6:'Sunday'}
        df.loc[df['day_name'].isna(), 'day_name'] = df['day_of_week'].map(day_name_map)
    else:
        # if it's already names/strings, normalize capitalization and use them
        df.loc[df['day_name'].isna(), 'day_name'] = df['day_of_week'].astype(str).str.strip().str.capitalize()

# final check: drop rows without a day name
df = df.dropna(subset=['day_name'])

# compute failure rate (%) and order days Mon->Sun
day_order = ['Monday','Tuesday','Wednesday','Thursday','Friday','Saturday','Sunday']
failure_rate_by_day_df = (df.groupby('day_name')['failure']
                           .mean()
                           .reindex(day_order)            # ensures chronological order, inserts NaN for missing days
                           .reset_index()
                           .rename(columns={'failure':'failure_rate'}) )
failure_rate_by_day_df['failure_rate_pct'] = failure_rate_by_day_df['failure_rate'] * 100
failure_rate_by_day_df = failure_rate_by_day_df.fillna(0)  # optional: set missing-day rates to 0

# plot using your existing barchart helper
barchart(data_df=failure_rate_by_day_df, x_col='day_name', y_col='failure_rate_pct',
         title='Failure Rate by Day of Week',
         xlabel='Day of Week', ylabel='Failure Rate (%)', rot_degrees=30)

Observations

  • Highest day: Friday — 4.66% failure rate (906 / 19,440).
  • Lowest day: Sunday — 1.26% failure rate (217 / 17,280).
  • Weekday vs weekend: Weekdays show substantially higher failure rates (Tue–Fri elevated), weekends lower — pattern suggests operational/maintenance scheduling influence.

Data Preprocessing¶

Splitting the data into train, validation, and test sets¶

This data is panel time-series: 15 turbines, each logged every 10 minutes over two months, and a single degradation episode spans many consecutive rows. A random split would scatter rows from the same episode across train and test, letting the model effectively see failures it is later scored on - inflating every metric.

Observations

  • The dataset contains 131,760 records and is sorted chronologically (then by turbine), which is appropriate for this panel time-series data and avoids leakage from randomly mixing related failure episodes.
  • A 70% / 15% / 15% chronological split was used.
  • Failure rates rise across time: 1.60% in training, 5.26% in validation, and 7.29% in test. This suggests failures become more common later in the observation period—possible evidence of degradation or temporal drift. It also confirms strong class imbalance.
  • failure, timestamp, and turbine_id are excluded from the model-input feature sets. Removing the target is required, and removing identifiers/timestamps helps avoid direct leakage.

Perform the following steps to handle missing values in the gearbox_oil_temp_C feature:

  1. Choose an imputation strategy (mean, median, or mode) based on the distribution of the feature.
  2. Calculate the selected statistic using only the training data.
  3. Use the calculated value to fill the missing values in the training, validation, and test datasets.
  4. Apply the same imputation value across all three datasets to ensure a consistent preprocessing strategy and prevent data leakage.

generator_bearing_temp_C¶

Perform the following steps to handle missing values in the generator_bearing_temp_C feature:

  1. Choose an imputation strategy (mean, median, or mode) based on the distribution of the feature.
  2. Calculate the selected statistic using only the training data.
  3. Use the calculated value to fill the missing values in the training, validation, and test datasets.
  4. Apply the same imputation value across all three datasets to ensure a consistent preprocessing strategy and prevent data leakage.

NOTE: Why Median - none of these distributions is symmetric. The two temperature variables are moderately right-skewed (skew ≈ 0.85), while oil pressure is strongly left-skewed (skew ≈ -1.77).

  • Their means are therefore pulled toward the tails—for example, gearbox-oil temperature mean is 58.21°C versus median 54.31°C.
  • The median is resistant to extreme operating/fault readings, so it is the safer and more representative fill value for these sensor variables.
  • Mode is less suitable because these are continuous measurements, where an exact repeated value has limited meaning.

Model Evaluation Criterion¶

In [ ]:

# metric_of_choice = 'accuracy'

# metric_of_choice = 'f1'

Utility Functions¶

Before moving ahead, we define a function to check the performance of the model using different metrics.

  • We will be using metric functions defined in sklearn for accuracy, precision, recall, f1_score
  • We will create a function which will print out all the above metrics in one go.
In [59]:
def model_performance_classification(model, predictors, target):
    """
    Function to compute different metrics to check classification model performance

    model: classifier (sklearn or tensorflow)
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    """

    # 1. Get raw predictions
    pred_raw = model.predict(predictors)

    # 2. Check the shape or values to handle DL vs ML models safely
    # If the predictions are probabilities (floats between 0 and 1, not exactly 0 or 1)
    # We check if any value falls strictly between 0 and 1
    if np.issubdtype(pred_raw.dtype, np.floating) and not np.all(np.isin(pred_raw, [0.0, 1.0])):
        # FOR TENSORFLOW DL MODELS: threshold the probabilities at 0.5
        pred = (pred_raw > 0.5).astype(int)
    else:
        # FOR SKLEARN ML MODELS: use them directly
        pred = pred_raw

    # Flatten predictions to ensure they match target shape perfectly
    pred = np.array(pred).flatten()

    # 3. Compute metrics
    acc = accuracy_score(target, pred)
    recall = recall_score(target, pred)
    precision = precision_score(target, pred)
    f1 = f1_score(target, pred)

    # 4. Creating a dataframe of metrics
    data_perf = pd.DataFrame(
        {"Accuracy": acc, "Recall": recall, "Precision": precision, "F1": f1},
        index=[0],
    )

    return data_perf
In [60]:
def plot_confusion_matrix(model, predictors, target):
    """
    To plot the confusion_matrix with percentages

    model: classifier
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    """
    # 1. Get raw predictions
    y_pred_raw = model.predict(predictors)

    # 2. Check if predictions are probabilities (typical for Keras/TF models or some ML models with predict_proba)
    # If y_pred_raw contains float values between 0 and 1, it's likely probabilities.
    if np.issubdtype(y_pred_raw.dtype, np.floating) and np.any((y_pred_raw > 0) & (y_pred_raw < 1)):
        # Binarize probabilities using a threshold (e.g., 0.5)
        y_pred = (y_pred_raw > 0.5).astype(int)
    else:
        # Use predictions directly (typical for scikit-learn classifiers that return binary labels)
        y_pred = y_pred_raw

    # Ensure y_pred is flattened to a 1D array, as confusion_matrix expects this format.
    y_pred = np.array(y_pred).flatten()

    cm = confusion_matrix(target, y_pred)
    labels = np.asarray(
        [
            ["{0:0.0f}".format(item) + "\n{0:.2%}".format(item / cm.flatten().sum())]
            for item in cm.flatten()
        ]
    ).reshape(2, 2)

    plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))
    sns.heatmap(cm, annot=labels, fmt="")
    plt.ylabel("True label")
    plt.xlabel("Predicted label")
    plt.show() # Added plt.show() to explicitly display the plot

Decision Tree Classifier¶

Perform the following steps to train and evaluate the Decision Tree model:

  1. Create a Decision Tree classifier using class_weight='balanced' to assign higher importance to the minority class and reduce the impact of class imbalance.
  2. Train the model using the training dataset.
  3. Evaluate the model on the training dataset by generating a confusion matrix and computing the performance metrics.
  4. Evaluate the model on the validation dataset by generating a confusion matrix and computing the performance metrics.
  5. Compare the training and validation results to assess how well the model generalizes and identify any signs of overfitting or underfitting.

# Convert the categorical day-of-week feature into numeric dummy variables.
# Align validation columns with training columns.
X_train_tree = pd.get_dummies(X_train, columns=['day_of_week'], dtype=int)
X_valid_tree = pd.get_dummies(X_valid, columns=['day_of_week'], dtype=int)

X_valid_tree = X_valid_tree.reindex(columns=X_train_tree.columns, fill_value=0)

# Create and train a class-balanced Decision Tree model.
dt_model = DecisionTreeClassifier(
    class_weight='balanced',
    random_state=42
)

dt_model.fit(X_train_tree, y_train)

# Training-set evaluation

display(dt_train_perf)

# Validation-set evaluation

print("Validation Performance Metrics")
dt_valid_perf = model_performance_classification(dt_model, X_valid_tree, y_valid)
display(dt_valid_perf)

# Compare model performance across the two splits
dt_comparison = pd.concat(
    [dt_train_perf, dt_valid_perf],
    keys=["Training", "Validation"]
)

display(dt_comparison)

Observations

  • The model achieves perfect performance on training data: accuracy, recall, precision, and F1-score are all 1.00. Its training confusion matrix has no errors.
  • On validation data, performance drops substantially:
    • Accuracy: 95.55%
    • Recall: 18.96%
    • Precision: 84.19%
    • F1-score: 30.95%
  • The model correctly identifies only 197 of 1,039 actual failures and misses 842 failures. This low recall is a major issue because the project aims to detect turbine failures.
  • The high validation accuracy is misleading because normal cases dominate the data. A model can be accurate overall while still failing to detect most of the minority failure class.
  • Precision is high, meaning that when the model predicts a failure, it is usually correct. However, it is too conservative in predicting failures.
  • The large gap between perfect training performance and weak validation recall/F1 indicates strong overfitting. The unrestricted Decision Tree memorizes patterns in the training data but does not generalize well to unseen data.

    • Precision: 51.82%
    • F1-score: 41.25%
  • The model correctly detects 356 of 1,039 failures, which is substantially better than the Decision Tree (197) and Random Forest (29) baselines. However, it still misses 683 failures, so recall needs improvement for a turbine-failure detection use case.
  • Unlike the previous models, Gradient Boosting shows less extreme overfitting: training performance is high, but validation F1-score remains meaningful rather than collapsing completely.
  • There is still a clear training–validation gap—especially in recall (94.5% to 34.3%) and F1 (93.8% to 41.3%)—which indicates moderate overfitting.
  • Validation accuracy is high but should not be the main selection metric because normal observations dominate the data. Validation recall and F1-score give a more realistic assessment.
  • Further tuning and imbalance handling using training sample_weight would likely help increase failure recall.

XGBoost¶

Perform the following steps to train and evaluate the XGBoost model:

  1. Calculate the number of negative and positive samples in the training data.
  2. Compute the scale_pos_weight value as the ratio of negative samples to positive samples to address class imbalance.
  3. Create an XGBoost classifier using the calculated scale_pos_weight and the selected random state.
  4. Train the model using the training dataset.
  5. Evaluate the model on the training dataset by generating a confusion matrix and computing the performance metrics.
  6. Evaluate the model on the validation dataset by generating a confusion matrix and computing the performance metrics.
  7. Compare the training and validation results to assess how well the model generalizes and identify any signs of overfitting or underfitting.
In [64]:
# Encode the categorical feature and align validation columns with training columns.
X_train_xgb = pd.get_dummies(X_train, columns=['day_of_week'], dtype=int)
X_valid_xgb = pd.get_dummies(X_valid, columns=['day_of_week'], dtype=int)

X_valid_xgb = X_valid_xgb.reindex(columns=X_train_xgb.columns, fill_value=0)

# Calculate class imbalance ratio using training labels only.
negative_samples = (y_train == 0).sum()
positive_samples = (y_train == 1).sum()

scale_pos_weight = negative_samples / positive_samples

print(f"Negative samples: {negative_samples}")
print(f"Positive samples: {positive_samples}")
print(f"scale_pos_weight: {scale_pos_weight:.2f}")

# Create and train the XGBoost model.
xgb_model = XGBClassifier(
    scale_pos_weight=scale_pos_weight,
    random_state=42,
    eval_metric="logloss"
)

xgb_model.fit(X_train_xgb, y_train)

# Training-set evaluation
print("Training Confusion Matrix")
plot_confusion_matrix(xgb_model, X_train_xgb, y_train)

print("Training Performance Metrics")
xgb_train_perf = model_performance_classification(xgb_model, X_train_xgb, y_train)
display(xgb_train_perf)

# Validation-set evaluation
print("Validation Confusion Matrix")
plot_confusion_matrix(xgb_model, X_valid_xgb, y_valid)

print("Validation Performance Metrics")
xgb_valid_perf = model_performance_classification(xgb_model, X_valid_xgb, y_valid)
display(xgb_valid_perf)

# Compare training and validation performance.
xgb_comparison = pd.concat(
    [xgb_train_perf, xgb_valid_perf],
    keys=["Training", "Validation"]
)

display(xgb_comparison)

Observations

  • The training data has 90,758 normal samples and 1,474 failure sample
  • scale_pos_weight is 61.57, meaning a failure observation receives about 62 times the weighting of a normal observation during training.
  • Training performance is perfect 100%.
  • Validation performance is the strongest among the baseline models:
    • Accuracy: 97.06%
    • Recall: 53.99%
    • Precision: 84.49%
    • F1-score: 65.88%
  • XGBoost identifies 561 of 1,039 actual failures and misses 478, making it much more effective at detecting failures than the earlier baseline Decision Tree, Random Forest, and Gradient Boosting models.
  • Its high precision means most failure alerts are reliable: only 103 normal cases are incorrectly flagged.
  • Despite excellent validation results, perfect training performance and lower validation recall/F1 indicate some overfitting. Still, the validation F1-score of 65.88% and recall of 53.99% show substantially better generalization than the other baseline models.
  • XGBoost is the best baseline candidate so far, particularly because it balances strong failure detection with few false alarms.

Perform the following steps to standardize the feature values:

  1. Create a StandardScaler object to standardize the numerical features.
  2. Fit the scaler using only the training dataset and transform the training features.
  3. Use the same fitted scaler to transform the validation and test datasets.
  4. Apply the same scaling parameters across all datasets to ensure a consistent preprocessing strategy and prevent data leakage.
In [66]:
# Identify numerical columns from the training dataset.
numerical_features = X_train.select_dtypes(include=['int64', 'float64']).columns

# Create the scaler.
scaler = StandardScaler()

# Fit only on training data, then transform each split using the same fitted scaler.
X_train_scaled = X_train.copy()
X_valid_scaled = X_valid.copy()
X_test_scaled = X_test.copy()

X_train_scaled[numerical_features] = scaler.fit_transform(
    X_train[numerical_features]
)

X_valid_scaled[numerical_features] = scaler.transform(
    X_valid[numerical_features]
)

X_test_scaled[numerical_features] = scaler.transform(
    X_test[numerical_features]
)

# Optional verification: training numerical features should have mean ~0 and std ~1.
print("Training feature means after scaling:")
display(X_train_scaled[numerical_features].mean().round(2).head())

print("Training feature standard deviations after scaling:")
display(X_train_scaled[numerical_features].std().round(2).head())

Perform the following steps to build the neural network architecture:

  1. Choose the number of neurons for the first hidden layer between 8 and 128.
    • Fewer neurons (8–32) create a simpler model that trains faster and is less likely to overfit.
    • More neurons (64–128) enable the model to learn more complex patterns but increase training time and the risk of overfitting.
  2. Choose an activation function for the first hidden layer (for example, relu, tanh, or sigmoid) based on the learning behavior you want.
  3. Create the output layer with a single neuron and a sigmoid activation function to predict the probability of the positive class.
In [68]:
# Neural networks require fully numeric inputs.
# Encode the categorical feature and align all feature columns.
X_train_nn = pd.get_dummies(X_train_scaled, columns=['day_of_week'], dtype=int)
X_valid_nn = pd.get_dummies(X_valid_scaled, columns=['day_of_week'], dtype=int)
X_test_nn = pd.get_dummies(X_test_scaled, columns=['day_of_week'], dtype=int)

X_valid_nn = X_valid_nn.reindex(columns=X_train_nn.columns, fill_value=0)
X_test_nn = X_test_nn.reindex(columns=X_train_nn.columns, fill_value=0)

# Build the neural network architecture.
ann_model = Sequential([
    tf.keras.Input(shape=(X_train_nn.shape[1],)),
    Dense(64, activation='relu'),     # First hidden layer
    Dense(1, activation='sigmoid')    # Output: predicted failure probability
])

Perform the following steps to configure the neural network for training:

  1. Choose an optimizer (sgd or adam) based on the desired training behavior.
    • sgd updates the model using simple gradient descent and may require more epochs to converge.
    • adam automatically adapts the learning rate, often converges faster, and is a common default choice.
  2. Use binary_crossentropy as the loss function since this is a binary classification problem.
  3. Configure the model to track Recall, Precision, and Binary Accuracy during training to evaluate its classification performance.
In [78]:
ann_model.compile(
    optimizer='adam',
    loss='binary_crossentropy',
    metrics=[
        tf.keras.metrics.Recall(name='recall'),
        tf.keras.metrics.Precision(name='precision'),
        tf.keras.metrics.BinaryAccuracy(name='binary_accuracy')
    ]
)

  • The ANN detects 448 of 1,039 failures and misses 591. Its recall is better than Gradient Boosting, but below XGBoost.
  • The model produces 210 false alarms, so precision is moderate rather than exceptionally high.
  • The sizeable drop from training F1 (90.34%) to validation F1 (52.79%) indicates overfitting, although the model still generalizes better than the Decision Tree and Random Forest baselines.
  • Accuracy should not be used as the main metric because normal observations dominate. Validation recall and F1-score are more meaningful for failure detection.

Baseline Model Performance Comparison¶

Training performance comparison¶

Perform the following steps to compare the training performance of all baseline models:

  1. Combine the training performance metrics of all baseline models into a single comparison table.
  2. Display the consolidated table to compare the performance of each model across the selected evaluation metrics.
  3. Use the comparison to identify the best-performing models for hyperparameter tuning.

Observations

  • XGBoost is the strongest baseline model. It has the best validation F1-score, recall, precision, and accuracy. It detects the highest proportion of failures while keeping false alerts low.
  • ANN is the second-best candidate. Its recall and F1-score are better than Gradient Boosting, but it raises more false alarms than XGBoost.
  • Gradient Boosting offers moderate validation performance but misses about two-thirds of failures, so it is a lower-priority tuning candidate.
  • Decision Tree and Random Forest should not be prioritized because their validation recall is very low—particularly Random Forest, which detects only about 3% of failures.
  • Perfect or near-perfect training results for Decision Tree, Random Forest, and XGBoost indicate overfitting risk. Validation F1 and recall are therefore more useful than training metrics or accuracy for selecting models.

Hyperparameter Tuning¶

Note: Choose at least two best-performing baseline models across the train and validation sets to proceed with tuning.

XGBoost¶

Perform the following steps to define the hyperparameter search space for the XGBoost model:

  1. Choose values for n_estimators, which controls the number of trees in the model. More trees can improve learning but increase training time.
  2. Choose values for learning_rate, which controls how quickly the model learns. Smaller values require more trees, while larger values learn faster but may overshoot.
  3. Choose values for max_depth, which controls the maximum depth of each tree. Deeper trees capture more complex patterns but are more likely to overfit.
  4. Choose values for min_child_weight, which controls the minimum weight required to create a new split. Larger values produce more conservative trees.
  5. Choose values for gamma, which specifies the minimum loss reduction required before making a split. Larger values reduce unnecessary splits.
  6. Choose values for subsample, which determines the fraction of training samples used to build each tree. Lower values improve generalization, while higher values use more data.
  7. Choose values for colsample_bytree, which specifies the fraction of features used to build each tree. Lower values increase diversity among trees.
  8. Choose values for reg_alpha and reg_lambda, which apply L1 and L2 regularization to reduce overfitting.
  9. Use the selected values to create the parameter grid for hyperparameter tuning and identify the best-performing model configuration.
In [90]:
# Define the XGBoost hyperparameter search space.
xgb_param_grid = {
    "n_estimators": [100, 200, 300, 500],
    "learning_rate": [0.01, 0.03, 0.05, 0.1],
    "max_depth": [3, 4, 5, 6],
    "min_child_weight": [1, 3, 5, 7],
    "gamma": [0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5],
    "subsample": [0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 1.0],
    "colsample_bytree": [0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 1.0],
    "reg_alpha": [0, 0.01, 0.1, 0.5],
    "reg_lambda": [0.5, 1, 2, 5]
}

Perform the following steps to tune the XGBoost model using randomized search:

  1. Perform randomized search with 5-fold cross-validation using the selected evaluation metric.
  2. Train the model on each sampled hyperparameter combination and evaluate its cross-validation performance.
  3. Display the best hyperparameter combination and its corresponding cross-validation score.
In [91]:
# Base estimator retains imbalance weighting derived from y_train only.
xgb_tuning_model = XGBClassifier(
    scale_pos_weight=scale_pos_weight,
    random_state=42,
    eval_metric="logloss",
    n_jobs=1
)

# Random search efficiently evaluates a subset of possible configurations.
xgb_random_search = RandomizedSearchCV(
    estimator=xgb_tuning_model,
    param_distributions=xgb_param_grid,
    n_iter=30,
    scoring="f1",
    cv=5,
    n_jobs=-1,
    verbose=1,
    random_state=42
)

# Fit only on training data.
xgb_random_search.fit(X_train_xgb, y_train)

# Best tuned XGBoost model and configuration.
best_xgb_model = xgb_random_search.best_estimator_

print("Best XGBoost parameters:")
print(xgb_random_search.best_params_)

print(f"\nBest cross-validation F1-score: {xgb_random_search.best_score_:.4f}")

Observations

  • XGBoost improved meaningfully after hyperparameter tuning, especially for failure detection.
  • The tuned model’s best 5-fold CV F1-score is 45.71%.
  • The selected configuration uses conservative, regularized trees: n_estimators=300, learning_rate=0.01, max_depth=4, min_child_weight=5, subsample=0.8, and colsample_bytree=0.8.
  • Validation recall rises from 53.99% to 73.24%. The tuned model detects about 200 additional failures compared with the baseline.
  • Validation F1 improves from 65.88% to 69.78%, making the tuned model more suitable for the failure-detection objective.
  • Precision falls from 84.49% to 66.64%, and accuracy decreases slightly. This means the improvement in detected failures comes with more false alerts—a reasonable trade-off when missed turbine failures are costly.
  • Overfitting is reduced. The baseline had perfect training metrics but lower validation F1; the tuned model has training F1 78.43% and validation F1 69.78%, a much smaller generalization gap.
  • Overall, the tuned XGBoost model is preferable to the baseline because it prioritizes finding failures while retaining a good validation F1-score.

Neural Networks¶

Perform the following steps to build the tuned neural network architecture:

  1. Choose the number of neurons and an activation function for the first hidden layer. Then apply Batch Normalization to stabilize training, followed by Dropout to reduce overfitting.
  2. Choose the number of neurons and an activation function for the second hidden layer. Again, apply Batch Normalization followed by Dropout to improve generalization.
  3. Create the output layer with a single neuron and a sigmoid activation function to predict the probability of the positive class.
  4. Review the selected architecture before proceeding with model training.
In [98]:
"""
The 64 → 32 neuron structure allows the network to learn progressively more focused patterns. 
ReLU is an efficient default activation, Batch Normalization stabilizes learning, and the dropout rates (0.30 and 0.20) help reduce overfitting.
"""

tuned_ann_model = Sequential([
    tf.keras.Input(shape=(X_train_nn.shape[1],)),

    # First hidden block
    Dense(64, activation='relu'),
    BatchNormalization(),
    Dropout(0.30),

    # Second hidden block
    Dense(32, activation='relu'),
    BatchNormalization(),
    Dropout(0.20),

    # Output layer: probability of turbine failure
    Dense(1, activation='sigmoid')
])

Perform the following steps to configure the tuned neural network for training:

  1. Choose an optimizer (adam or sgd) based on the desired training behavior.
    • adam automatically adapts the learning rate, often converges faster, and is a common default choice.
    • sgd updates the model using simple gradient descent and may require more epochs to converge.
  2. Use binary_crossentropy as the loss function since this is a binary classification problem.
  3. Configure the model to track Recall, Precision, and Binary Accuracy during training to evaluate its classification performance.
In [100]:
#using adam optimizer
tuned_ann_model.compile(
    optimizer='adam',
    loss='binary_crossentropy',
    metrics=[
        tf.keras.metrics.Recall(name='recall'),
        tf.keras.metrics.Precision(name='precision'),
        tf.keras.metrics.BinaryAccuracy(name='binary_accuracy')
    ]
)

  2. Select a batch size between 16 and 128 based on the available computational resources and training behavior.

Observations

  • The tuned ANN improves validation recall by 15.88 percentage points and F1-score by 9.78 percentage points.
  • It identifies about 613 of 1,039 failures and misses about 426. This is a clear improvement over the baseline ANN.
  • Precision falls only slightly (from 68.09% to 66.63%), so the improved failure detection comes with a modest increase in false alerts.
  • Training metrics remain stronger than validation metrics: training F1 is 80.39%, versus validation F1 of 62.58%. This indicates some remaining overfitting, but the Batch Normalization and Dropout architecture provides better validation generalization than the baseline.
  • The tuned ANN is a strong improvement over the baseline ANN. However, tuned XGBoost remains the better overall model so far, with higher validation recall (73.24%) and F1-score (69.78%)

Decision Tree¶

Perform the following steps to define the hyperparameter search space for the Decision Tree model:

  1. Choose the splitting criterion (gini or entropy) to determine how the model selects the best feature at each split.
  2. Choose values for max_depth to control the maximum depth of the tree. Deeper trees can capture more complex patterns but are more likely to overfit.
  3. Choose values for min_samples_split to control the minimum number of samples required to split a node. Larger values create more conservative trees.
  4. Choose values for min_samples_leaf to control the minimum number of samples required in each leaf node. Larger values produce smoother and more generalized trees.
  5. Choose the max_features strategy (sqrt or log2) to control how many features are considered when searching for the best split.
  6. Use the selected values to create the parameter grid for hyperparameter tuning and identify the best-performing model configuration.
In [108]:
# Define the Decision Tree hyperparameter search space.
dt_param_grid = {
    "criterion": ["gini", "entropy"],
    "max_depth": [3, 5, 7, 10, 15, 20, None],
    "min_samples_split": [2, 5, 10, 20, 50],
    "min_samples_leaf": [1, 2, 5, 10, 20],
    "max_features": ["sqrt", "log2"]
}

Perform the following steps to tune the Decision Tree model using randomized search:

  1. Perform randomized search with 5-fold cross-validation using the selected evaluation metric.
  2. Train the model on each sampled hyperparameter combination and evaluate its cross-validation performance.
  3. Display the best hyperparameter combination and its corresponding cross-validation score.
In [109]:
# Perform randomized hyperparameter tuning using 5-fold cross-validation.
dt_random_search = RandomizedSearchCV(
    estimator=dt_model,
    param_distributions=dt_param_grid,
    n_iter=30,
    scoring="f1",
    cv=5,
    n_jobs=-1,
    verbose=1,
    random_state=42
)

# Fit the randomized search on training data only.
start = time.time()

dt_random_search.fit(X_train_tree, y_train)

end = time.time()

# Retrieve the best Decision Tree configuration.
best_dt_model = dt_random_search.best_estimator_

print("Best Decision Tree Parameters:")
print(dt_random_search.best_params_)

print(f"\nBest 5-Fold Cross-Validation F1-score: "
      f"{dt_random_search.best_score_:.4f}")

print(f"Tuning time: {end - start:.2f} seconds")

Observations

  • The tuned tree identifies all validation failures: 1,039 out of 1,039. This is valuable where missed turbine failures are very costly.
  • However, precision is low. It generates approximately 1,470 false alerts, so many predicted failures are normal turbine states.
  • Compared with the baseline Decision Tree, validation recall improves sharply—from 18.96% to 100%—and F1 improves from 30.95% to 58.57%. Accuracy and precision decrease because the tuned model flags far more observations as failures.
  • The shallow depth (max_depth=3) and minimum leaf size (20) successfully reduce the extreme memorization of the baseline tree. Training and validation F1-scores are relatively close, so there is no strong sign of overfitting.
  • Although this tuned tree has the highest recall, tuned XGBoost remains the stronger balanced choice overall because it has a higher validation F1-score (69.78%) with substantially fewer false alerts.

Random Forest¶

Perform the following steps to define the hyperparameter search space for the Random Forest model:

  1. Choose values for n_estimators, which controls the number of trees in the forest. More trees generally improve stability but increase training time.
  2. Choose values for max_depth to control the maximum depth of each tree. Deeper trees capture more complex patterns but are more likely to overfit.
  3. Choose values for min_samples_split to control the minimum number of samples required to split a node. Larger values create more conservative trees.
  4. Choose values for min_samples_leaf to control the minimum number of samples required in each leaf node. Larger values improve generalization by preventing overly specific splits.
  5. Choose the max_features strategy (sqrt or log2) to control how many features are considered when searching for the best split in each tree.
  6. Use the selected values to create the parameter grid for hyperparameter tuning and identify the best-performing model configuration.
In [113]:

    "min_samples_split": [2, 5, 10, 20, 50],
    "min_samples_leaf": [1, 2, 5, 10, 20],
    "max_features": ["sqrt", "log2"]
}

Gradient Boosting¶

Perform the following steps to define the hyperparameter search space for the Gradient Boosting model:

  1. Choose values for n_estimators, which controls the number of boosting stages. More boosting stages can improve learning but increase training time.
  2. Choose values for learning_rate, which controls how quickly the model learns. Smaller values require more boosting stages, while larger values learn faster but may overfit.
  3. Choose values for max_depth to control the maximum depth of each decision tree. Deeper trees capture more complex patterns but are more likely to overfit.
  4. Choose values for subsample, which determines the fraction of training samples used for each boosting stage. Lower values improve generalization by introducing randomness, while higher values use more data for learning.
  5. Choose the max_features strategy (sqrt or log2) to control how many features are considered when searching for the best split in each tree.
  6. Use the selected values to create the parameter grid for hyperparameter tuning and identify the best-performing model configuration.
In [116]:

    "subsample": [0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 1.0],
    "max_features": ["sqrt", "log2"]
}

  • The baseline Decision Tree, Random Forest, and XGBoost all achieve perfect training scores (100% across every metric). This is a strong indication that these baseline models memorized the training data and may overfit.
  • Baseline Gradient Boosting (93.84% F1) and baseline ANN (90.34% F1) also have very high training performance.

    • Gradient Boosting: 93.84% → 89.81%
    • ANN: 90.34% → 80.39%
  • Tuned Gradient Boosting has the highest training F1-score among the tuned models (89.81%), followed by the tuned ANN (80.39%).
  • Training metrics alone should not determine the final model. The key evidence of successful tuning is whether the lower training scores are accompanied by better validation F1 and recall—which is particularly true for the tuned Random Forest and XGBoost models.

Observations

  • Tuned Random Forest is the best overall model, with the highest validation F1-score (74.86%), highest accuracy (97.34%), and strong recall (75.36%) and precision (74.36%). It provides the best balance between detecting failures and avoiding unnecessary alerts.
  • Tuned XGBoost is the second-best model: F1 69.78% and recall 73.24%. It catches many failures, but has lower precision than the tuned Random Forest.

    • ANN: 52.80% → 62.58%
  • The tuned Decision Tree achieves 100% recall, so it detects every validation failure. However, precision is only 41.41%, meaning it creates many false alerts; its F1 is therefore lower than Random Forest and XGBoost.
  • The untuned Random Forest performs especially poorly (recall 2.79%), showing severe overfitting. Tuning transforms it into the best-generalizing model.
  • Accuracy is high for most models because normal records dominate. F1-score, recall, and precision are more useful for choosing the final failure-detection model.
  • Based on this comparison, the tuned Random Forest is the appropriate final model, with tuned XGBoost as the strongest alternative.

Feature Importance¶

In [122]:
def plot_feature_importances(model, X, y, feature_names=None, color="violet", figsize=(10, 10)):
    """
    Plots feature importances for both Traditional ML models (XGBoost, RF)
    and Deep Learning models (ANNs).

    Parameters:
    - model: Trained model object (XGBoost, Sklearn, Keras wrapper, etc.)
    - X: Evaluation features (DataFrame or 2D array)
    - y: Evaluation targets (Series or 1D array)
    - feature_names: List of feature names. If None and X is a DataFrame, uses X.columns.
    """
    # 1. Automatically grab feature names if not provided
    if feature_names is None:
        if hasattr(X, 'columns'):
            feature_names = X.columns
        else:
            feature_names = [f"Feature {i}" for i in range(X.shape[1])]

    # Convert X to numpy if it's a DataFrame for permutation calculation safety
    X_val = X.values if hasattr(X, 'columns') else X

    # 2. Extract or calculate importances
    if hasattr(model, 'feature_importances_'):
        print("💡 Detected Tree-based model. Extracting built-in feature importances...")
        importances = model.feature_importances_
        title = "Feature Importances (Tree-based Model)"
        xlabel = "Relative Importance"
    else:
        print("💡 Detected ANN/Black-box model. Calculating Permutation Importance...")
        # n_repeats is how many times a feature is shuffled; higher is more accurate but slower
        result = permutation_importance(model, X_val, y, n_repeats=5, random_state=42)
        importances = result.importances_mean
        title = "Feature Importances (Permutation Importance - ANN)"
        xlabel = "Mean Performance Drop when Shuffled"

    # 3. Sort the importances in ascending order
    indices = np.argsort(importances)

    # 4. Plotting
    plt.figure(figsize=figsize)
    plt.title(title)
    plt.barh(range(len(indices)), importances[indices], color=color, align="center")
    plt.yticks(range(len(indices)), [feature_names[i] for i in indices])
    plt.xlabel(xlabel)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

Observations

  • Of 1,440 actual failures, the model correctly detects 629 but misses 811.
  • It raises approximately 1,078 failure alerts, of which about 449 are false alerts.
  • Test performance is notably weaker than validation performance (validation F1 74.86%, recall 75.36%). This suggests the model generalizes less effectively to the later unseen time period, likely due to temporal drift and the higher test failure rate.
  • Accuracy remains relatively high because normal records are still the majority class; recall and F1 are more meaningful for this failure-detection problem.
  • The model is a useful baseline, but its real-world result shows that it misses more than half of failures. But we need to consider threshold tuning and retraining with more recent data / time-aware validation.

Why Tuned XGBoost Was Also Evaluated on the Test Set¶

Although the tuned Random Forest achieved the best validation performance, Tuned XGBoost was evaluated as an additional final benchmark because it was the second-best validation model and showed strong failure-detection capability.

On the test dataset, Tuned XGBoost achieved higher recall and F1-score than the tuned Random Forest. This means it identified more actual turbine failures, which is important because missed failures can result in unplanned downtime and costly repairs. While XGBoost generated more false alerts, its stronger ability to detect failures makes it a more suitable model for the predictive-maintenance objective.

Note: Since the test dataset was evaluated for both final candidates, it has now informed model selection. A new untouched holdout dataset should be used for a fully unbiased future performance estimate.

Business Insights and Recommendations¶

Business Insights¶

  • Failure risk increases over time. The failure rate rises from 1.60% in training data to 7.29% in the test period, indicating possible asset degradation or temporal drift. This makes periodic retraining essential.
  • Vibration and lubrication signals are strong failure indicators. Failed turbines show higher drivetrain vibration and elevated oil-particle counts. These signals are physically consistent with bearing wear, gearbox damage, and lubrication-system degradation.
  • Failures often occur during lower-output states. Failed turbines have lower median power output (about 137 kW) than normal turbines (about 201 kW). Reduced generation combined with abnormal condition-monitoring signals is a meaningful warning pattern.

Recommendations¶

  • Deploy the Tuned Random Forest as a maintenance-prioritization tool. Use its predicted failure alerts to rank turbines for inspection, rather than making automatic shutdown decisions.
  • Create a technician triage workflow. Investigate alerts with high vibration, high oil-particle counts, abnormal bearing/oil temperatures, and low power output first. This helps manage the model’s false-alert volume.
  • Monitor and retrain the model regularly. Track recall, precision, F1-score, alert volume, and confirmed maintenance outcomes. Retrain with recent SCADA and maintenance data to account for temporal drift.
  • Retain existing safety and maintenance controls. The model still misses some failures, so SCADA alarms, scheduled maintenance, and engineering inspections must remain in place alongside model predictions.
